verses.13:4: But the King of kings aroused the anger of Antiochus against the wicked wretch, and when Lysias pointed out that this man was the cause of the evils, indeed of all of them, he ordered them to take him to Beroea and put him to death, as is the custom in that place.
verses.13:5: Now in that place there is a tower fifty cubits high, full of ashes, and it had a circular contrivance sloping steeply on every side down into the ashes.
verses.13:6: There everyone pushes forward to destruction anyone guilty of sacrilege, or who has also committed an extreme degree of any other evils.
verses.13:7: By such a doom it happened that the lawless Menelaus died, not even obtaining burial in the earth;
verses.13:8: and very justly so: for since he had committed many sins concerning the altar, whose fire and ashes were pure, in ashes he received his death.
verses.13:9: Now the king was coming, weighed down in his thoughts, intending to inflict on the Jews the worst of the things that had happened in the time of his father.
verses.13:10: But when Judas learned of these things, he ordered the multitude to call upon the Lord day and night, that if ever at any other time, now also He would come to the aid of those who were about to be deprived of the law, their homeland, and the holy temple,
verses.13:11: and not to allow the people, who had only just briefly been revived, to fall under the power of the blasphemous nations.
verses.13:12: When all had done the same together and implored the merciful Lord with weeping, fasting, and prostration for three days without ceasing, Judas encouraged them and commanded them to present themselves.
verses.13:13: And meeting privately with the elders, he resolved that before the king's army could invade Judea and become masters of the city, they would march out and decide the matter with the help of God.
verses.13:14: So committing the decision to the Lord of the world, and urging those with him to fight nobly even to death for laws, temple, city, homeland, and commonwealth, he stationed his army around Modein.
verses.13:15: And giving to those with him the watchword, "Victory of God," he attacked the royal pavilion by night with the finest chosen young men, struck down the camp to about two thousand men, and brought down the foremost of the elephants together with the one in its housing.
verses.13:16: And finally they filled the camp with terror and confusion, and withdrew successfully.
verses.13:17: Now this had taken place as day was already beginning to dawn, because of the Lord's protection that came to his aid.
verses.13:18: Now the king, having had a taste of the boldness of the Jews, made attempts on the positions by stratagems,
verses.13:19: and against Beth-zur, a small fortress of the Jews. He advanced, was routed, met with a setback, was defeated.
verses.13:20: And Judas sent in what was needed to those inside.
verses.13:21: But Rhodocus, from the Jewish ranks, reported the secrets to the enemies; he was sought out and caught and locked up.
verses.13:22: The king negotiated a second time with those in Beth-zur, gave the right hand, received it, departed, attacked Judas and his men, was worsted,
verses.13:23: learned that Philip, who had been left in charge of affairs, had lost his senses in Antioch, was dismayed, appealed to the Jews, yielded, and swore to all the just terms, came to a settlement and offered a sacrifice, honored the sanctuary and the place, showed kindness,
verses.13:24: and welcomed Maccabeus, left Hegemonides as governor from Ptolemais as far as the Genneri,
verses.13:25: came to Ptolemais. The people of Ptolemais were indignant about the agreements, for they were exceedingly afraid; they wanted to annul the stipulations.
verses.13:26: Lysias stepped up to the platform, made the best possible defense, persuaded and calmed them, made them favorably disposed, broke camp for Antioch. Thus went the affairs of the king's advance and withdrawal.
verses.14:1: Now after a three-year period, word reached Judas and those with him that Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, having sailed in through the harbor at Tripolis with a strong force and a fleet,
verses.14:2: had taken control of the country, having put to death Antiochus and his guardian Lysias.
verses.14:3: Now a certain Alcimus, who had formerly been high priest, but had willfully defiled himself in the times of separation, realizing that there was no safety for him in any way at all, nor any longer access to the holy altar,
verses.14:4: came to King Demetrius about the one hundred and fifty-first year, presenting to him a gold crown and a palm branch, and in addition to these, some of the customary olive branches of the temple. And on that day he kept quiet.
verses.14:5: But having found an opportunity aiding his own folly, when he was summoned to a council by Demetrius and asked in what disposition and intention the Jews stood, in answer to these things he said,
verses.14:6: "Those among the Jews who are called Hasideans, whom Judas Maccabeus leads, keep up war and stir up sedition, not allowing the kingdom to attain stability.
verses.14:7: Therefore, deprived of my ancestral glory, meaning the high priesthood, I have now come a second time,
verses.14:8: first, genuinely concerned for the things pertaining to the king, and second, also having regard for my own fellow citizens; for by the recklessness of the aforementioned men, our entire nation suffers misfortune to no small degree.
verses.14:9: Now you, king, having ascertained each of these matters, make provision for both the country and our hard-pressed nation, in accordance with the gracious kindness that you have toward all.
verses.14:10: For as long as Judas remains alive, it is impossible for affairs to attain peace."
verses.14:11: When such things had been spoken by him, the rest of the friends, being hostilely disposed toward Judas, quickly inflamed Demetrius still further.
verses.14:12: And immediately selecting Nicanor, who had been commander of the elephants, and appointing him governor of Judea, he sent him out,
verses.14:13: giving written orders to put Judas himself to death, to scatter those with him, and to establish Alcimus as high priest of the greatest temple.
verses.14:14: And the Gentiles in Judea who had fled from Judas joined Nicanor in droves, thinking that the misfortunes and calamities of the Jews would be their own prosperity.
verses.14:15: Now when they heard of the advance of Nicanor and the assault of the Gentiles, sprinkling earth upon themselves, they implored Him who established His people forever and always with a manifestation comes to the aid of His own portion.
verses.14:16: And when the leader gave the order, immediately setting out from there, he engaged them at the village of Lessau.
verses.14:17: Now Simon, the brother of Judas, had encountered Nicanor in battle, yet slowly, because of the sudden consternation of the adversaries, had suffered a setback.
verses.14:18: Nevertheless, Nicanor, hearing of the valor that Judas and those with him possessed and their courage in the struggles for their homeland, was reluctant to make the decision by bloodshed.
verses.14:19: Therefore he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to give and receive right-hand pledges.
verses.14:20: And when lengthy deliberation about these matters had taken place, and the leader had consulted with the troops, and unanimous consent appeared, they assented to the treaty.
verses.14:21: And they appointed a day on which they would come to the same place privately. And a litter came forward from each one; they set out seats.
verses.14:22: Judas stationed armed men ready in the strategic places, in case treachery should suddenly arise from the enemies. They held the appropriate conference.
verses.14:23: Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing improper, and he dismissed the crowds that had gathered in droves.
verses.14:24: And he kept Judas continually in his presence; he had become devoted to the man from his very soul.
verses.14:25: He urged him to marry and have children; he married, settled down, shared in life.
verses.14:26: But Alcimus, observing their goodwill toward one another and taking the treaty that had been made, came to Demetrius and kept saying that Nicanor held sentiments alien to the affairs of state, for he had appointed Judas, the conspirator against his kingdom, as successor.
verses.14:27: Then the king, becoming enraged and provoked by the slanders of that utterly wicked man, wrote to Nicanor, stating that he was greatly displeased about the treaty, and commanding him to send Maccabeus as a prisoner to Antioch quickly.
verses.14:28: When these things reached Nicanor, he was dismayed and deeply distressed that he would violate what had been stipulated, though the man had done nothing wrong.
verses.14:29: Yet since it was not possible to oppose the king, he watched for an opportune time to carry this out by a stratagem.
verses.14:30: But Maccabeus, observing that Nicanor had been acting more harshly in his dealings with him and had become more rude in their customary meeting, realizing that this harshness did not come from the best motive, gathered together not a few of those with him and went into hiding from Nicanor.
verses.14:31: When the other realized that he had been boldly outmaneuvered by the man, he came to the greatest and holy temple while the priests were offering the prescribed sacrifices, and he commanded them to hand over the man.
verses.14:32: And when they declared with oaths that they did not know at all where the one being sought was,
verses.14:33: stretching out his right hand toward the sanctuary, he swore these words: "Unless you hand Judas over to me as a prisoner, I will make this sacred enclosure of God into flat ground, and I will demolish the altar, and here I will erect a splendid temple to Dionysus."
verses.14:34: Having spoken such words, he departed. And the priests, stretching out their hands toward heaven, called upon the continual defender of our nation, saying,
verses.14:35: "You, Lord, being in need of nothing at all, were pleased that a sanctuary of Your dwelling should come to be among us.
verses.14:36: And now, holy Lord of all sanctification, keep undefiled forever this house that has recently been purified."
verses.14:37: Now a certain Razis, one of the elders from Jerusalem, was denounced to Nicanor, a man devoted to his fellow citizens and very well spoken of, and because of his goodwill called father of the Jews.
verses.14:38: For in the earlier times of separation he had incurred charges of Judaism, and had risked both body and soul for Judaism with all earnestness.
verses.14:39: Now Nicanor, wishing to make evident the hostility that he had toward the Jews, sent more than five hundred soldiers to arrest him.
verses.14:40: For he thought that by arresting that man he would inflict a calamity upon them.
verses.14:41: When the troops were about to capture the tower and were forcing the courtyard door, ordering fire to be brought and the doors to be set ablaze, being surrounded on every side, he turned the sword upon himself,
verses.14:42: wishing to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of the wicked and be subjected to outrages unworthy of his own nobility.
verses.14:43: But having missed his mark with the blow because of the haste of the struggle, and while the crowds were bursting inside the doorways, he ran bravely up onto the wall and hurled himself down courageously into the crowds.
verses.14:44: And as they quickly stepped back and a space opened up, he landed right in the middle of the empty space.
verses.14:45: Still breathing and inflamed with rage, he rose up while blood gushed out in torrents and his wounds were severe, and ran through the crowds; and standing upon a steep rock,
verses.14:46: now becoming completely drained of blood, he pulled out his entrails, and taking them in both hands, hurled them at the crowds; and calling upon Him who rules over life and spirit to give these same things back to him again, in this manner he died.
verses.15:1: Now Nicanor, having learned that Judas and those with him were in the places around Samaria, planned to attack them with complete security on the day of rest.
verses.15:2: When the Jews who were accompanying him under compulsion said, "By no means destroy them so savagely and barbarously, but give glory to the day that has been preeminently honored with holiness by the One who watches over all things,"
verses.15:3: the thrice-accursed man asked whether there is in heaven the Sovereign who has commanded that the Sabbath day be kept.
verses.15:4: When they declared, "There is the living Lord Himself, Sovereign in heaven, who ordered that the seventh day be observed,"
verses.15:5: the other said, "And I too am a sovereign on the earth, who commands that arms be taken up and the royal duties be carried out." Nevertheless, he did not succeed in carrying out his wicked purpose.
verses.15:6: And Nicanor, holding his head high with complete security, had resolved to establish a common manner for Judas and those with him.
verses.15:7: But Maccabeus was unceasingly confident, with all hope, that he would obtain help from the Lord.
verses.15:8: And he encouraged those with him not to fear the assault of the nations, but, keeping in mind the former acts of help that had come to them from heaven, to expect now as well the victory that would come to them from the Almighty.
verses.15:9: And comforting them from the Law and the Prophets, and also praising them and the struggles that they had completed, he made them more eager.
verses.15:10: And rousing them in their spirits, he gave his orders, at the same time pointing out the faithlessness of the nations and the violation of oaths.
verses.15:11: And arming each one of them not so much with the security of shields and spears as with the encouragement in good words, and relating in addition a trustworthy dream, he gladdened them all exceedingly.
verses.15:12: Now the vision of it was like this: Onias, who had been high priest, a noble and good man, modest in demeanor, gentle in manner, uttering speech fittingly, and from childhood having thoroughly practiced all things proper to virtue—this man stretched out his hands and was praying for the whole community of the Jews.
verses.15:13: Then next there appeared a man distinguished by gray hair and glory, and the dignity surrounding him was something marvelous and most majestic.
verses.15:14: And Onias answered and said, "This is the one who loves his brothers, who prays much for the people and the holy city, Jeremiah, the prophet of God."
verses.15:15: Then Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and handed to Judas a golden sword, and as he gave it, he spoke these words:
verses.15:16: "Take the holy sword, a gift from God, through which you will shatter the adversaries."
verses.15:17: Having been encouraged by the words of Judas, which were altogether noble and able to spur them on to valor and to embolden the souls of young men, they resolved not to carry on a campaign, but gallantly to rush in, and engaging at close quarters with all bravery to decide the matter, because the city and the holy things and the temple were in danger.
verses.15:18: For their fear for wives and children, and furthermore for brothers and relatives, held a lesser place with them, while greatest and first was their fear for the consecrated sanctuary.
verses.15:19: And for those confined in the city as well, there was no slight distress, as they were troubled over the clash in the open field.
verses.15:20: And when all were already awaiting the coming decision, and the enemies had already closed in and the army had been drawn up in array, and the beasts had been stationed in a favorable position, and the cavalry had been arrayed on the flank,
verses.15:21: Maccabeus, observing the presence of the multitudes and the varied equipment of arms, and the ferocity of the beasts in a favorable position, stretched out his hands to heaven and called upon the wonder-working Lord, knowing that it is not through arms, but that as it is decided by Him, He secures victory for the worthy.
verses.15:22: And calling upon Him, he spoke in this manner: "You, Master, sent Your angel in the time of Hezekiah, king of Judea, and he killed as many as one hundred eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib.
verses.15:23: And now, Sovereign of the heavens, send a good angel before us for dread and trembling;
verses.15:24: by the greatness of Your arm, may those who come with blasphemy against Your holy people be struck with terror." And he ended with these words.
verses.15:25: Now Nicanor and those with him were advancing with trumpets and battle songs.
verses.15:26: But Judas and those with him engaged the enemies with invocation and prayers.
verses.15:27: And fighting with their hands while praying to God with their hearts, they struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand, greatly gladdened by the care of God.
verses.15:28: And when they had finished the engagement and were returning with joy, they recognized Nicanor lying fallen in his full armor.
verses.15:29: And when a shout and commotion arose, they blessed the Sovereign in their ancestral language.
verses.15:30: And he who was in everything, in body and soul, the foremost champion on behalf of the citizens, who had preserved the goodwill of his youth toward his countrymen, commanded that they cut off the head of Nicanor, and his arm along with the shoulder, and carry them around to Jerusalem.
verses.15:31: And when he arrived there and had called together his countrymen and stationed the priests before the altar, he sent for those from the citadel.
verses.15:32: And having displayed the head of the vile Nicanor and the arm of the blasphemer, which he had stretched out against the holy house of the Almighty as he boasted arrogantly,
verses.15:33: and having cut out the tongue of the impious Nicanor, he ordered it in pieces for the birds, and the wages of his folly to be hung opposite the sanctuary.
verses.15:34: And toward heaven they all blessed the manifest Lord, saying, "Blessed is the One who has preserved His own place undefiled."
verses.15:35: And he hung the severed head of Nicanor from the citadel, clearly visible to all and an evident sign of the help of the Lord.
verses.15:36: And they all decreed by a public resolution by no means to leave this day unmarked, but to keep as a marked day the thirteenth of the twelfth month (it is called Adar in the Lord's language), one day before the day of Mordecai.
verses.15:37: Since, then, the affairs concerning Nicanor turned out in this way, and from those times the city was held by the Hebrews, I myself will also bring my account to an end right here.
verses.15:38: And if it is well done, aptly in its composition, this is what I myself also wished; but if poorly and moderately, this was what was attainable for me.
verses.15:39: Just as drinking wine by itself, and likewise water on the other hand, is harmful, whereas in the way that wine mixed with water now also produces a delightful pleasure, so also the crafting of the account delights the ears of those who read the composition. And here will be the end.

notes.1:8: The Greek text reads ἐξηγάγομεν ("brought out"), whereas other Greek witnesses read ἐξήψαμεν ("lit").
notes.1:10: The Greek text reads "eighty-eighth year" (ἔτους ὀγδοηκοστοῦ καὶ ὀγδόου) and attaches "in Jerusalem" to the date, whereas other Greek witnesses read "one hundred eighty-eighth year" and begin the greeting with "Those in Jerusalem."
notes.1:12: The Greek text places "into Persia" (εἰς τὴν Περσίδα) at the end of verse 12 rather than at the beginning of verse 13 as in some other editions.
notes.1:35: The Greek text omits the verb "showed favor" (ἐχαρίζετο) found in other Greek witnesses, leaving a compressed relative construction.
notes.1:36: The Greek text reads Νεφθάρ ("Nephthar") in both occurrences, whereas other Greek witnesses read Νεφθάι ("Nephthai") in the second.
notes.2:17: The Greek opens with a nominative participial phrase (ὁ δὲ θεὸς ὁ σώσας...) that shifts without a finite verb into the causal clause of verse 18 (ἐλπίζομεν γάρ); it is rendered here as a nominal clause.
notes.2:25: The Greek text reads φιλοφρονοῦσιν ("who take pleasure / are favorably inclined"), whereas other Greek witnesses read φιλοπονοῦσιν ("who labor diligently").
notes.2:28: The Greek text reads ἀτονοῦντες ("growing weary / being weak"), whereas other Greek witnesses read διαπονοῦντες ("striving / laboring diligently").
notes.2:29: The Greek text reads ἐνκαινίζειν ("to dedicate"), whereas other Greek witnesses read ἐγκαίειν ("to paint in encaustic").
notes.3:11: The Greek text contains an elliptical participial clause ("οὐχ οὕτως διαβάλλων ὁ δυσσεβὴς Σίμων", lit. "not thus falsely accusing, the impious Simon"), contrasting Onias's account with Simon's report; other manuscripts read "οὕτως δ' ἦν διαβάλλων" ("thus the impious Simon was slandering") or "οὐχ ὡς διέβαλλεν" ("not as ... was slandering").
notes.3:18: The Greek text retains the negative "μή" ("διὰ τὸ μὴ μέλλειν"), giving a purpose sense ("so that the place would not be about to come into contempt"), whereas some manuscripts omit "μή" ("because the place was about to come into contempt").
notes.3:21: The Greek text has the bare infinitive "ἐλεεῖν δέ" (lit. "and to pity..."), rendered "And one had to pity...", whereas other manuscripts read "ἐλεεινὸν δ' ἦν" ("and it was pitiable").
notes.3:26: The Greek text reads "κάλλιστοι δὲ τὴν γλῶσσαν" ("finest in speech" or "in tongue"), where other manuscripts read "τὴν δόξαν" ("in splendor" or "in glory").
notes.3:28: The Greek text uses the accusative singular participle "ἐπεγνωκότα" (referring to Heliodorus) and reads simply "τὴν δυναστίαν" ("the sovereign power"), whereas other manuscripts read the plural "ἐπεγνωκότες" and add "τοῦ θεοῦ" ("of God").
notes.4:4: The Greek text reads "Coele-Phoenicia and Syria" (as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read the more usual "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia."
notes.4:5: The Greek text reads diekosmethe ("prepared himself [to go]," as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read diekomisthe ("made his way" or "traveled").
notes.4:12: The Greek text reads ton eph' hemon ("those of our time," as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read ton ephebon ("the youths/ephebes"). "The broad-brimmed hat" translates petason, the Greek hat worn by ephebes and associated with Hermes.
notes.4:20: The Greek text preserves a shorter reading (as in Codex Alexandrinus) that omits intervening clauses found in other witnesses and reads "on account of those present" (ton paronton) rather than "on account of the bearers" (ton parakomizonton).
notes.4:33: The Greek text reads apenegken ("reported it" or "brought charges," as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read apelegchen ("exposed" or "rebuked him").
notes.5:3: The Greek text reads kamaton ("toils/struggles"), a reading found in Codex Alexandrinus; other manuscripts read kamakon ("spear-shafts" or "pikes").
notes.5:8: The Greek text reads enkleistheis ("imprisoned" or "confined"); other manuscripts read enkletheis ("accused").
notes.5:10: The Greek text reads patroou nomou ("ancestral law"); other manuscripts read patroou taphou ("ancestral tomb").
notes.5:20: The Greek text reads katalephtheis ("overtaken" or "seized"); other manuscripts read kataleiphtheis ("forsaken" or "abandoned").
notes.5:26: The Greek text reads katestesen ("stationed" or "posted"); other manuscripts read katestrosen ("struck down" or "killed"), referring to great multitudes of the city's inhabitants.
notes.6:1: Greek geronta Athenaion may mean "an elderly Athenian," "an Athenian senator," or a proper name, "Geron the Athenian."
notes.6:2: Greek Dios xeniou ("Zeus Xenios") refers to Zeus as patron of hospitality and strangers. The Greek text reads etynchanon ("happened to be"), linking the title to the character of the inhabitants; other manuscripts read enetynchanon ("petitioned" or "requested").
notes.6:19: Greek tympanon refers to a drum-shaped wheel or wooden rack on which victims were stretched and beaten to death.
notes.6:23: The Greek text reads politeias ("way of life" or "citizenship"); other manuscripts read polias ("gray hair").
notes.6:29: The Greek text uses a compact construction (agonton ... eumeneian dysmeneian, literally "bringing goodwill [to] ill will"); other manuscripts expand this explicitly with eis ... metabalonton ("turning goodwill into ill will").
notes.7:11: The Greek text reads "have been called" (kekletai), whereas many manuscripts read "I have acquired" or "received" (kektemai).
notes.7:18: The Greek text reads "any further" (mallon), where other manuscripts read "in vain" (maten).
notes.7:21: The Greek text reads "each of the men" (ton anthropon), whereas other manuscripts read "each of them" (auton).
notes.7:28: Literally "not out of things that exist" (ouk ex onton), a phrase frequently discussed in relation to creation out of nothing.
notes.7:37: The Greek text reads "fortune" (tychen) and the plural participle "as we call upon" (epikaloumenoi), whereas other manuscripts read "soul" (psychen) and the singular participle (epikaloumenos).
notes.8:16: The Greek text reads "the prisoners" (tois desmiois, as in Codex Alexandrinus), where other witnesses read "the enemies" (tous polemious).
notes.8:20: The Greek text reads "the six thousand" (hoi hexakischilioi, as in Codex Alexandrinus), differing from the "eight thousand" stated earlier in the verse (which other witnesses repeat here).
notes.8:23: The Greek text places "Eleazar" in the accusative as part of the preceding list of leaders, with the nominative participle "having read aloud" referring to Judas; other textual traditions construe Eleazar as the reader of the sacred book.
notes.8:26: The Greek text reads "custom" (dike, as in Codex Alexandrinus), where other witnesses read "hour" (hora) or "afternoon" (deile); similarly in v. 25, the Greek text reads "from the region" (apo tes choras) rather than "by the hour" (hypo tes horas).
notes.8:34: The Greek text reads "three thousand" (trischilious, as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read "one thousand" (chilious).
notes.9:8: The Greek text reads "presumed against the waves of the sea" (antidokon tois tes thalasses kumasin, as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read "just now thought he could command the waves of the sea" (arti dokon ... epitassein).
notes.9:12: The Greek text reads "think arrogant thoughts" (hyperephana phronein, as in Codex Alexandrinus), whereas other witnesses read "think himself equal to God" (isothea phronein).
notes.9:15: The Greek text reads "to destroy" (ektripsai, as in Codex Alexandrinus), where other witnesses read "to cast out" (ekripsai).
notes.9:20: The Greek text reads "Be well ... and your own affairs will be" (as in Codex Alexandrinus), omitting the conditional "if" and the clause "we give the greatest thanks" found in other witnesses.
notes.9:24: The Greek text reads "should also go forth" (prosapelthe, as in Codex Alexandrinus), where other witnesses read "should be reported" (prosangelthe).
notes.10:4: The Greek text omits the infinitive "to be disciplined" (paideuesthai) found in some manuscripts after "with gentleness," leaving an elliptical clause supplied here as "to be dealt with."
notes.10:8: The Greek text reads "the tenth days" (tas dekatas hemeras), whereas other witnesses read "these days" (tasde tas hemeras) by a different word division.
notes.10:10: The Greek text reads "the supreme Antiochus" (ton hypaton, a variant for the royal epithet "Eupator" that appears in v. 13) and "of the cities" (ton poleon), where other manuscripts read "of the wars" (ton polemon).
notes.10:14: The Greek text reads "against his own people" (pros tous idious), whereas other manuscripts read "against the Jews" (pros tous Ioudaious).
notes.10:33: The Greek text reads "forty days" here and "the twenty-fifth day" in v. 35 (with no numeral before "young men"), whereas other manuscripts read "four days" here and "the fifth day, twenty young men" in v. 35.
notes.11:5: A schoinos was an ancient unit of distance equal to roughly three to four miles, making five schoinoi approximately fifteen to twenty miles, matching the distance from Jerusalem to Beth-zur. Some Greek manuscripts read stadia instead.
notes.11:15: The Greek text reads "the scribe" (grammateus, or "secretary"), whereas many other witnesses read "the king" (basileus).
notes.11:21: Dios Corinthius is an unusual month name not otherwise attested in the Macedonian calendar and is often regarded as a variant form of the month Dios or Dioskoros.
notes.11:23: The Greek text reads the genitive participle "desiring" (agreeing with "our father") and "of the Jews," whereas other witnesses read the nominative plural "desiring" (referring to the king) and "of their own affairs."
notes.11:31: The Greek text reads "expenditures" (dapanemasin), whereas other manuscripts read "dietary practices" (diaitemasin).
notes.12:13: The Greek word gephyroun ('built with causeways/bridges') is textually difficult; other manuscripts and editors read 'with bridges/earthworks' or interpret it as a place name, Gephyrun.
notes.12:20: The Greek text reads literally 'two thousand and in addition to the seven thousand,' whereas other Greek manuscripts read 'two thousand five hundred.'
notes.12:27: Unlike some Greek manuscripts that mention Lysias dwelling in Ephron, the Greek text translated here mentions only the multitudes of all tribes in the city.
notes.12:28: The Greek text reads holkas (literally 'weights' or 'forces'), an early manuscript variant for alkas ('strength' or 'might').
notes.12:45: The Greek text reads eite ('or if') and eucharisterion (literally 'thank-offering' or 'gracious reward'), a variant for charisterion ('reward').
notes.13:9: The Greek text reads bebaremenos ('weighed down' or 'burdened'), whereas other Greek manuscripts read bebarbaromenos ('barbarous' or 'filled with savage intentions').
notes.13:15: The Greek text reads synetheken (literally 'put together' or 'brought down together'), where other manuscripts read synekentesen ('pierced through'); 'in its housing' refers to the wooden battle tower mounted on the elephant's back.
notes.13:19: The Greek text reads oligon ('small'), whereas other Greek manuscripts read ochyron ('strong' or 'fortified').
notes.13:24: The Greek text reads ton Genneron ('the Genneri'), a manuscript variant for ton Gerrenon ('the Gerrenians').
notes.13:25: The Greek text reads edeiliazon ('were afraid'), whereas other Greek manuscripts read edeinopathoun ('were deeply aggrieved' or 'indignant').
notes.14:7: The Greek text reads the middle participle aphelomenos (here rendered "deprived of," where other manuscripts read apheimenos) and deuteron ("a second time," where other manuscripts read deuro, "here").
notes.14:16: The Greek text preserves the place name Lessau (Lessaou), whereas some Greek manuscripts read Dessau (Dessaou).
notes.14:17: The Greek text reads bradeos ("slowly," where other manuscripts read bracheos, "slightly"), and the rare noun aphasian literally means "speechlessness" or "consternation," with "of the adversaries" variously taken as dismay caused by or occurring among the opponents.
notes.14:21: The Greek word diphrax ("litter") occurs only here in ancient Greek and is understood as a litter, sedan chair, or chariot brought forward from each side.
notes.14:44: The Greek noun keneon ("empty space") matches the preceding "space opened up," though the same word can also denote the anatomical hollow of the flank or abdomen.
notes.15:6: The Greek text here reads asphaleias ('security') and tropon ('manner'), whereas other witnesses read alazoneias ('arrogance') and tropaion ('trophy/monument').
notes.15:17: The Greek text reads me strateuesthai ('not to carry on a campaign') and enpheresthai ('to rush in'), where other witnesses read me stratopedeuesthai ('not to encamp') and epipheresthai ('to attack').
notes.15:27: The Greek text reads epimeleia ('care'), whereas other witnesses read epiphaneia ('manifestation').
notes.15:33: The Greek text omits an explicit verb before 'for the birds' (where other witnesses add dosein, 'would give') and reads meta meros ('in pieces') for kata meros. The term 'wages' (epicheira, linked to cheir, 'hand/arm') plays on Nicanor's severed arm.
notes.15:36: The Greek text reads kyriake ('the Lord's') for the language naming the month Adar, whereas other witnesses read Syriake ('Syrian,' i.e., Aramaic).
